div2.stage: [Music.] Enter Orsino Duke of Illyria, Curio, and other Lords.

lg.l: If music be the food of love, play on,
Give me excess of it, that surfeiting,
The appetite may sicken, and so die.
[To the Musicians] That strain again! It had a dying fall;
Oh, it came o'er my ear like the sweet sound
That breathes upon a bank of violets,
Stealing, and giving odor. [To the Musicians] Enough, no more.
'Tis not so sweet now as it was before.
O spirit of love, how quick and fresh art thou,
That notwithstanding thy capacity
Receiveth as the sea, nought enters there,
Of what validity and pitch soe'er,
But falls into abatement and low price
Even in a minute. So full of shapes is fancy,
That it alone is high fantastical.
Will you go hunt, my Lord?
What, Curio?
The hart.
Why so I do, the noblest that I have.
O when mine eyes did see Olivia first,
Methought she purged the air of pestilence;
That instant was I turned into a hart,
And my desires, like fell and cruel hounds,
E'er since pursue me.
How now, what news from her?
So please my lord, I might not be admitted,
But from her handmaid do return this answer:
The element itself, till seven years' heat,
Shall not behold her face at ample view;
But like a cloistress she will veilèd walk,
And water once a day her chamber round
With eye-offending brine—all this to season
A brother's dead love, which she would keep fresh
And lasting in her sad remembrance.
O she that hath a heart of that fine frame
To pay this debt of love but to a brother,
How will she love, when the rich golden shaft
Hath killed the flock of all affections else
That live in her—when liver, brain, and heart,
These sovereign thrones, are all supplied, and filled
Her sweet perfections, with one self king!
Away before me, to sweet beds of flowers;
Love-thoughts lie rich, when canopied with bowers.

div2.stage: Enter Viola, a Captain, and Sailors[as from a shipwreck].

lg.l: What country, friends, is this?
This is Illyria, lady.
And what should I do in Illyria?
My brother he is in Elysium.
Perchance he is not drowned—what think you, sailors?
It is perchance that you yourself were saved.
Oh, my poor brother! And so perchance may he be.
True, madam, and to comfort you with chance,
Assure your self, after our ship did split,
When you, and those poor number saved with you,
Hung on our driving boat, I saw your brother,
Most provident in peril, bind himself—
Courage and hope both teaching him the practice—
To a strong mast, that lived upon the sea;
Where, like Arion on the dolphin's back,
I saw him hold acquaintance with the waves
So long as I could see.
[Giving him gold] For saying so, there's gold.
Mine own escape unfoldeth to my hope,
Whereto thy speech serves for authority,
The like of him. Know'st thou this country?
Ay, madam, well, for I was bred and born
Not three hours' travel from this very place.
Who governs here?
A noble duke, in nature as in name.
What is his name?
Orsino.
Orsino! I have heard my father name him.
He was a bachelor then.
And so is now, or was so very late;
For but a month ago I went from hence,
And then 'twas fresh in murmur (as you know,
What great ones do, the less will prattle of)
That he did seek the love of fair Olivia.
What's she?
A virtuous maid, the daughter of a count
That died some twelvemonth since, then leaving her
In the protection of his son, her brother,
Who shortly also died; for whose dear love,
They say, she hath abjured the sight
And company of men.
Oh, that I served that lady,
And might not be delivered to the world
Till I had made mine own occasion mellow,
What my estate is!
That were hard to compass,
Because she will admit no kind of suit,
No, not the duke's.
There is a fair behavior in thee, Captain;
And though that nature with a beauteous wall
Doth oft close in pollution, yet of thee
I will believe thou hast a mind that suits
With this thy fair and outward character.
I prithee—and I'll pay thee bounteously—
Conceal me what I am, and be my aid
For such disguise as haply shall become
The form of my intent. I'll serve this duke.
Thou shalt present me as an eunuch to him—
It may be worth thy pains, for I can sing,
And speak to him in many sorts of music,
That will allow me very worth his service.
What else may hap, to time I will commit,
Only shape thou thy silence to my wit.
Be you his eunuch, and your mute I'll be;
When my tongue blabs, then let mine eyes not see.
I thank thee. Lead me on.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Toby [booted], and Maria[with a light].

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: What a plague means my niece to take the death of her brother thus! I am sure care's an enemy to life.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: By my troth, Sir Toby, you must come in earlier a-nights. Your cousin, my lady, takes great exceptions to your ill hours.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Why let her except, before excepted.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Ay, but you must confine yourself within the modest limits of order.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Confine? I'll confine myself no finer than I am! These clothes are good enough to drink in, and so be these boots too; an they be not, let them hang themselves in their own straps.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: That quaffing and drinking will undo you. I heard my lady talk of it yesterday—and of a foolish knight that you brought in one night here, to be her wooer.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Who, Sir Andrew Aguecheek?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Ay, he.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: He's as tall a man as any's in Illyria.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: What's that to th'purpose?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Why, he has three thousand ducats a year.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Ay, but he'll have but a year in all these ducats. He's a very fool, and a prodigal.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Fie that you'll say so! He plays o'th'viol-de-gamboys, and speaks three or four languages word for word without book, and hath all the good gifts of nature.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: He hath indeed, all most natural. For besides that he's a fool, he's a great quarreler; and but that he hath the gift of a coward, to allay the gust he hath in quarreling, 'tis thought among the prudent he would quickly have the gift of a grave.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: By this hand, they are scoundrels and substractors that say so of him. Who are they?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: They that add, moreover, he's drunk nightly in your company.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: With drinking healths to my niece! I'll drink to her as long as there is a passage in my throat, and drink in Illyria. He's a coward and a coistrel that will not drink to my niece till his brains turn o'th'toe, like a parish top. Enter Sir Andrew. What, wench! Castiliano vulgo ; for here comes Sir Andrew Agueface.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Sir Toby Belch! How now, Sir Toby Belch!

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Sweet Sir Andrew!

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Bless you, fair shrew.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: And you too, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Accost, Sir Andrew, accost!

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: My niece's chambermaid.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Good Mistress Accost, I desire better acquaintance.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: My name is Mary, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Good Mistress Mary Accost—

p.seg: You mistake, knight. "Accost" is front her, board her, woo her, assail her.
By my troth, I would not undertake her in this company. Is that the meaning of "accost"?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Fare you well, gentlemen.

p.seg: An thou let part so, Sir Andrew, would thou might'st never draw sword again.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: An you part so, mistress, I would I might never draw sword again! Fair lady, do you think you have fools in hand?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Sir, I have not you by th'hand.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Marry, but you shall have, and here's my hand.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: [Taking his hand] Now sir, thought is free. I pray you, bring your hand to th'buttery bar, and let it drink.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Wherefore, sweetheart? What's your metaphor?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: It's dry, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Why, I think so. I am not such an ass but I can keep my hand dry. But what's your jest?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: A dry jest, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Are you full of them?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Ay, sir, I have them at my fingers' ends. [Letting go his hand] Marry, now I let go your hand, I am barren.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: O knight, thou lack'st a cup of canary. [Pouring wine] When did I see thee so put down?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Never in your life, I think, unless you see canary put me down. Methinks sometimes I have no more wit than a Christian or an ordinary man has. But I am a great eater of beef, and I believe that does harm to my wit.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: No question.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: An I thought that, I'd forswear it. I'll ride home tomorrow, Sir Toby.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Pourquoi , my dear knight?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: What is pourquoi ? "Do," or "not do"? I would I had bestowed that time in the tongues that I have in fencing, dancing, and bear-baiting. O had I but followed the arts!

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Then hadst thou had an excellent head of hair.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Why, would that have mended my hair?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Past question, for thou see'st it will not curl by nature.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: But it becomes me well enough, dost not?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Excellent! It hangs like flax on a distaff; and I hope to see a housewife take thee between her legs, and spin it off.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Faith, I'll home tomorrow, Sir Toby. Your niece will not be seen, or if she be, it's four to one she'll none of me. The count himself here hard by woos her.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: She'll none o'th'count. She'll not match above her degree, neither in estate, years, nor wit; I have heard her swear't. Tut, there's life in't, man.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: I'll stay a month longer. I am a fellow o'th' strangest mind i'th'world. I delight in masques and revels sometimes altogether.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Art thou good at these kickshawses, knight?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: As any man in Illyria, whatsoever he be, under the degree of my betters; and yet I will not compare with an old man.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: What is thy excellence in a galliard, knight?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Faith, I can cut a caper.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: And I can cut the mutton to it.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: And I think I have the back-trick simply as strong as any man in Illyria.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Wherefore are these things hid? Wherefore have these gifts a curtain before 'em? Are they like to take dust, like Mistress Moll's picture? Why dost thou not go to church in a galliard, and come home in a coranto? My very walk should be a jig; I would not so much as make water but in a cinquepace! What dost thou mean! Is it a world to hide virtues in? I did think by the excellent constitution of thy leg, it was formed under the star of a galliard.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Ay, 'tis strong, and it does indifferent well in a flame-colored stock. Shall we set about some revels?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: What shall we do else? Were we not born under Taurus!

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Taurus? That's sides and heart.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: No, sir, it is legs and thighs. Let me see thee caper. [Sir Andrew dances.] Ha, higher! Ha, ha, excellent!

div2.stage: Enter Valentine, and Viola in man's attire [as Cesario].

sp.speaker: VALENTINE
sp.p: If the Duke continue these favors towards you, Cesario, you are like to be much advanced. He hath known you but three days, and already you are no stranger.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: You either fear his humor, or my negligence, that you call in question the continuance of his love. Is he inconstant, sir, in his favors?

sp.speaker: VALENTINE
sp.p: No, believe me.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: I thank you. Here comes the count.

sp.speaker: ORSINO
sp.p: Who saw Cesario, ho?

lg.l: On your attendance, my lord, here.
[To the Courtiers] Stand you awhile aloof. [All but Viola stand apart.] Cesario,
Thou know'st no less but all; I have unclasped
To thee the book even of my secret soul.
Therefore, good youth, address thy gait unto her,
Be not denied access, stand at her doors,
And tell them, there thy fixèd foot shall grow
Till thou have audience.
Sure, my noble lord,
If she be so abandoned to her sorrow
As it is spoke, she never will admit me.
Be clamorous, and leap all civil bounds,
Rather than make unprofited return.
Say I do speak with her, my lord, what then?
O then unfold the passion of my love,
Surprise her with discourse of my dear faith;
It shall become thee well to act my woes,
She will attend it better in thy youth,
Than in a nuncio's [Indicating Valentine] of more grave aspect.
I think not so, my lord.
Dear lad, believe it;
For they shall yet belie thy happy years
That say thou art a man. Diana's lip
Is not more smooth, and rubious; thy small pipe
Is as the maiden's organ, shrill, and sound;
And all is semblative a woman's part.
I know thy constellation is right apt
For this affair. [To the Courtiers] Some four or five attend him—
All if you will, for I myself am best
When least in company. Prosper well in this,
And thou shalt live as freely as thy lord
To call his fortunes thine.
I'll do my best
To woo your lady. [Exit Orsino.] [To the audience] Yet a barful strife;
Whoe'er I woo, myself would be his wife.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Nay, either tell me where thou hast been, or I will not open my lips so wide as a bristle may enter, in way of thy excuse. My lady will hang thee for thy absence.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Let her hang me; he that is well hanged in this world needs to fear no colors.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Make that good.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: He shall see none to fear!

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: A good lenten answer. I can tell thee where that saying was born, of "I fear no colors."

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Where, good Mistress Mary?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: In the wars; and that may you be bold to say in your foolery.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Well, God give them wisdom that have it; and those that are fools, let them use their talents.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Yet you will be hanged for being so long absent; or to be turned away—is not that as good as a hanging to you?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Many a good hanging prevents a bad marriage; and for turning away, let summer bear it out.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: You are resolute, then?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Not so neither, but I am resolved on two points—

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: That if one break, the other will hold; or if both break, your gaskins fall!

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Apt in good faith, very apt. Well, go thy way; if Sir Toby would leave drinking, thou wert as witty a piece of Eve's flesh as any in Illyria.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Peace, you rogue, no more o'that! Enter Lady Olivia, with Malvolio [and Gentlemen] [and Ladies]. Here comes my lady. Make your excuse wisely, you were best.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: [To the audience] Wit, an't be thy will, put me into good fooling! Those wits that think they have thee, do very oft prove fools; and I, that am sure I lack thee, may pass for a wise man. For what says Quinapalus? "Better a witty fool, than a foolish wit." [To Olivia] God bless thee, lady!

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: [To the Gentlemen] Take the fool away.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Do you not hear, fellows? Take away the lady.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Go to, y'are a dry fool; I'll no more of you. Besides, you grow dishonest.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Two faults, madonna, that drink and good counsel will amend: for give the dry fool drink, then is the fool not dry. Bid the dishonest man mend himself: if he mend, he is no longer dishonest; if he cannot, let the botcher mend him. Anything that's mended is but patched; virtue that transgresses is but patched with sin, and sin that amends is but patched with virtue. If that this simple syllogism will serve, so; if it will not, what remedy? As there is no true cuckold but calamity, so beauty's a flower. The lady bade take away the fool, therefore I say again, take her away.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Sir, I bade them take away you.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Misprision in the highest degree! Lady, cucullus non facit monachum —that's as much to say, as "I wear not motley in my brain." Good madonna, give me leave to prove you a fool.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Can you do it?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Dexteriously, good madonna.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Make your proof.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: I must catechize you for it, madonna. Good my mouse of virtue, answer me.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Well sir, for want of other idleness, I'll bide your proof.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Good madonna, why mourn'st thou?

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Good fool, for my brother's death.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: I think his soul is in hell, madonna.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: I know his soul is in heaven, fool.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: The more fool, madonna, to mourn for your brother's soul, being in heaven. [To the Gentlemen] Take away the fool, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: What think you of this fool, Malvolio? Doth he not mend?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Yes, and shall do, till the pangs of death shake him: infirmity, that decays the wise, doth ever make the better fool.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: God send you, sir, a speedy infirmity, for the better increasing your folly: Sir Toby will be sworn that I am no fox, but he will not pass his word for twopence that you are no fool.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: How say you to that, Malvolio?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: I marvel your ladyship takes delight in such a barren rascal. I saw him put down the other day with an ordinary fool, that has no more brain than a stone. Look you now, he's out of his guard already. Unless you laugh and minister occasion to him, he is gagged. I protest I take these wise men, that crow so at these set kind of fools, no better than the fools' zanies.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Oh, you are sick of self-love, Malvolio, and taste with a distempered appetite. To be generous, guiltless, and of free disposition, is to take those things for bird-bolts that you deem cannon bullets. There is no slander in an allowed fool, though he do nothing but rail; nor no railing in a known discreet man, though he do nothing but reprove.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Now Mercury endue thee with leasing, for thou speak'st well of fools.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Madam, there is at the gate a young gentleman much desires to speak with you.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: From the Count Orsino, is it?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: I know not, madam. 'Tis a fair young man, and well attended.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Who of my people hold him in delay?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Sir Toby, madam, your kinsman.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Fetch him off, I pray you, he speaks nothing but madman. Fie on him! [Exit Maria.] Go you, Malvolio; if it be a suit from the count, I am sick, or not at home. What you will, to dismiss it. Exit Malvolio. Now you see, sir, how your fooling grows old, and people dislike it.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Thou hast spoke for us, madonna, as if thy eldest son should be a fool; whose skull Jove cram with brains, for— Enter Sir Toby [drunk]. here he comes— one of thy kin has a most weak pia mater.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: By mine honor, half drunk. What is he at the gate, cousin?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: A gentleman.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: A gentleman? What gentleman?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: 'Tis a gentleman here— [belching] a plague o'these pickle herring! [To Clown] How now, sot!

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Good Sir Toby!

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Cousin, cousin, how have you come so early by this lethargy?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Lechery? I defy lechery! There's one at the gate.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Ay, marry, what is he?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Let him be the devil an he will, I care not; give me faith, say I. Well, it's all one.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: What's a drunken man like, fool?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Like a drowned man, a fool, and a madman: one draught above heat makes him a fool, the second mads him, and a third drowns him.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Go thou and seek the coroner, and let him sit o'my coz, for he's in the third degree of drink: he's drowned. Go look after him.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: He is but mad yet, madonna, and the fool shall look to the madman.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Madam, yond young fellow swears he will speak with you. I told him you were sick; he takes on him to understand so much, and therefore comes to speak with you. I told him you were asleep; he seems to have a foreknowledge of that too, and therefore comes to speak with you. What is to be said to him, lady? He's fortified against any denial.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Tell him he shall not speak with me.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: He has been told so; and he says he'll stand at your door like a sheriff's post, and be the supporter to a bench, but he'll speak with you.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: What kind o'man is he?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Why, of mankind.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: What manner of man?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Of very ill manner: he'll speak with you, will you or no.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Of what personage and years is he?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Not yet old enough for a man, nor young enough for a boy: as a squash is before 'tis a peascod, or a codling when 'tis almost an apple. 'Tis with him in standing water between boy and man. He is very well-favored, and he speaks very shrewishly; one would think his mother's milk were scarce out of him.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Let him approach. Call in my gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: [Calling offstage] Gentlewoman, my lady calls.

lg.l: Give me my veil. Come, throw it o'er my face.
We'll once more hear Orsino's embassy.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: The honorable lady of the house, which is she?

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Speak to me, I shall answer for her. Your will?

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Most radiant, exquisite, and unmatchable beauty— [To Maria or a Gentleman] I pray you tell me if this be the lady of the house, for I never saw her. I would be loath to cast away my speech; for besides that it is excellently well penned, I have taken great pains to con it. [Olivia and others laugh.] Good beauties, let me sustain no scorn; I am very comptible, even to the least sinister usage.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Whence came you, sir?

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: I can say little more than I have studied, and that question's out of my part. Good gentle one, give me modest assurance if you be the lady of the house, that I may proceed in my speech.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Are you a comedian?

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: No, my profound heart; and yet—by the very fangs of malice I swear—I am not that I play. Are you the lady of the house?

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: If I do not usurp myself, I am.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Most certain, if you are she, you do usurp yourself, for what is yours to bestow is not yours to reserve. But this is from my commission. I will on with my speech in your praise, and then show you the heart of my message.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Come to what is important in't, I forgive you the praise.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Alas, I took great pains to study it, and 'tis poetical.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: It is the more like to be feigned, I pray you keep it in. I heard you were saucy at my gates, and allowed your approach rather to wonder at you, than to hear you. If you be not mad, be gone. If you have reason, be brief. 'Tis not that time of moon with me to make one in so skipping a dialogue.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Will you hoist sail, sir? Here lies your way.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: [To Maria] No, good swabber, I am to hull here a little longer. [To Olivia] Some mollification for your Giant, sweet lady! Tell me your mind, I am a messenger.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Sure you have some hideous matter to deliver, when the courtesy of it is so fearful. Speak your office.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: It alone concerns your ear. I bring no overture of war, no taxation of homage. I hold the olive in my hand. My words are as full of peace as matter.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Yet you began rudely. What are you? What would you?

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: The rudeness that hath appeared in me, have I learned from my entertainment. What I am, and what I would, are as secret as maidenhead: to your ears, divinity; to any others', profanation.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Give us the place alone; we will hear this divinity. [Exeunt Maria, Gentlemen, and Ladies.] Now sir, what is your text?

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Most sweet lady—

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: A comfortable doctrine, and much may be said of it. Where lies your text?

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: In Orsino's bosom.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: In his bosom! In what chapter of his bosom?

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: To answer by the method, in the first of his heart.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: O, I have read it. It is heresy. Have you no more to say?

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Good madam, let me see your face.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Have you any commission from your lord to negotiate with my face? You are now out of your text. But we will draw the curtain, and show you the picture. [She unveils.] Look you, sir, such a one I was this present. Is't not well done?

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Excellently done, if god did all.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: 'Tis in grain, sir, 'twill endure wind and weather.

lg.l: 'Tis beauty truly blent, whose red and white
Nature's own sweet and cunning hand laid on.
Lady, you are the cruel'st she alive
If you will lead these graces to the grave,
And leave the world no copy.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: O sir, I will not be so hardhearted. I will give out divers schedules of my beauty. It shall be inventoried, and every particle and utensil labeled to my will: as, item, [Indicating] two lips, indifferent red; item, two grey eyes, with lids to them; item, one neck; one chin; and so forth. Were you sent hither to praise me?

lg.l: I see you what you are, you are too proud;
But if you were the devil, you are fair.
My lord and master loves you. O, such love
Could be but recompensed, though you were crowned
The nonpareil of beauty.
How does he love me?
With adorations, fertile tears,
With groans that thunder love, with sighs of fire.
Your lord does know my mind, I cannot love him.
Yet I suppose him virtuous, know him noble,
Of great estate, of fresh and stainless youth;
In voices well divulged, free, learn'd, and valiant,
And in dimension, and the shape of nature,
A gracious person. But yet I cannot love him.
He might have took his answer long ago.
If I did love you in my master's flame,
With such a suff'ring, such a deadly life,
In your denial I would find no sense;
I would not understand it.
Why, what would you?
Make me a willow cabin at your gate,
And call upon my soul within the house;
Write loyal cantos of contemnèd love,
And sing them loud even in the dead of night;
Hallow your name to the reverberate hills,
And make the babbling gossip of the air
Cry out "Olivia!" O you should not rest
Between the elements of air and earth,
But you should pity me.
You might do much!
What is your parentage?
Above my fortunes, yet my state is well:
I am a gentleman.
Get you to your lord.
I cannot love him. Let him send no more,
Unless, perchance, you come to me again,
To tell me how he takes it. Fare you well.
[Offering a purse] I thank you for your pains. Spend this for me.
I am no fee'd post, lady; keep your purse.
My master, not myself, lacks recompense.
Love make his heart of flint, that you shall love,
And let your fervor, like my master's, be
Placed in contempt. Farwell, fair cruelty.
"What is your parentage?"
"Above my fortunes, yet my state is well:
I am a gentleman." I'll be sworn thou art!
Thy tongue, thy face, thy limbs, actions, and spirit,
Do give thee five-fold blazon. Not too fast! Soft, soft!
Unless the master were the man. How now!
Even so quickly may one catch the plague?
Methinks I feel this youth's perfections
With an invisible and subtle stealth
To creep in at mine eyes. Well, let it be.
[Calling] What ho, Malvolio!
Here, madam, at your service.
Run after that same peevish messenger,
The county's man. He left this ring behind him,
lg.stage: [Having secretly taken a ring from her finger, she gives it to Malvolio.]
lg.l: Would I or not. Tell him I'll none of it.
Desire him not to flatter with his lord,
Nor hold him up with hopes; I am not for him.
If that the youth will come this way tomorrow,
I'll give him reasons for't. Hie thee, Malvolio.
Madam, I will.
[To the audience] I do I know not what, and fear to find
Mine eye too great a flatterer for my mind.
Fate, show thy force, ourselves we do not owe;
What is decreed must be; and be this so.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Will you stay no longer? Nor will you not that I go with you?

sp.speaker: SEBASTIAN
sp.p: By your patience, no. My stars shine darkly over me. The malignancy of my fate might perhaps distemper yours; therefore I shall crave of you your leave that I may bear my evils alone. It were a bad recompense for your love to lay any of them on you.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Let me yet know of you whither you are bound.

sp.speaker: SEBASTIAN
sp.p: No, sooth, sir. My determinate voyage is mere extravagancy. But I perceive in you so excellent a touch of modesty that you will not extort from me what I am willing to keep in; therefore it charges me in manners the rather to express myself. You must know of me then, Antonio, my name is Sebastian (which I called Roderigo). My father was that Sebastian of Messaline whom I know you have heard of. He left behind him myself and a sister, both born in an hour. If the heavens had been pleased, would we had so ended! But you, sir, altered that, for some hour before you took me from the breach of the sea was my sister drowned.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Alas the day!

sp.speaker: SEBASTIAN
sp.p: A lady, sir, though it was said she much resembled me, was yet of many accounted beautiful. But though I could not with such estimable wonder overfar believe that, yet thus far I will boldly publish her: she bore a mind that envy could not but call fair. [Weeping] She is drowned already, sir, with salt water, though I seem to drown her remembrance again with more.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: Pardon me, sir, your bad entertainment.

sp.speaker: SEBASTIAN
sp.p: O good Antonio, forgive me your trouble.

sp.speaker: ANTONIO
sp.p: If you will not murder me for my love, let me be your servant.

sp.speaker: SEBASTIAN
sp.p: If you will not undo what you have done—that is, kill him whom you have recovered—desire it not. Fare ye well at once; my bosom is full of kindness, and I am yet so near the manners of my mother that upon the least occasion more mine eyes will tell tales of me. I am bound to the Count Orsino's court; farewell.

lg.l: The gentleness of all the gods go with thee!
I have many enemies in Orsino's court,
Else would I very shortly see thee there.
But come what may, I do adore thee so
That danger shall seem sport, and I will go.

div2.stage: Enter Viola [as Cesario] and Malvolio [with the ring], at several doors.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Were not you even now with the Countess Olivia?

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Even now, sir; on a moderate pace, I have since arrived but hither.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: She returns this ring to you, sir. You might have saved me my pains to have taken it away yourself. She adds, moreover, that you should put your lord into a desperate assurance she will none of him. And one thing more: that you be never so hardy to come again in his affairs, unless it be to report your lord's taking of this. [Offering the ring] Receive it so.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: She took the ring of me; I'll none of it.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Come, sir, you peevishly threw it to her; and her will is, it should be so returned. [Throwing the ring down] If it be worth stooping for, there it lies, in your eye; if not, be it his that finds it.

lg.l: [To the audience] [Picking up the ring] I left no ring with her. What means this lady?
Fortune forbid my outside have not charmed her!
She made good view of me; indeed so much
That methought her eyes had lost her tongue,
For she did speak in starts distractedly.
She loves me, sure; the cunning of her passion
Invites me in this churlish messenger.
None of my lord's ring? Why, he sent her none;
I am the man! If it be so, as 'tis,
Poor lady, she were better love a dream.
Disguise, I see thou art a wickedness,
Wherein the pregnant enemy does much.
How easy is it for the proper false
In women's waxen hearts to set their forms.
Alas, our frailty is the cause, not we,
For such as we are made of, such we be.
How will this fadge? My master loves her dearly
And I, poor monster, fond as much on him,
And she, mistaken, seems to dote on me.
What will become of this? As I am man,
My state is desperate for my master's love;
As I am woman—now alas the day—
What thriftless sighs shall poor Olivia breathe?
O time, thou must untangle this, not I,
It is too hard a knot for me t'untie.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Toby and Sir Andrew.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Approach, Sir Andrew. Not to be abed after midnight, is to be up betimes; and diluculo surgere , thou know'st.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Nay, by my troth, I know not; but I know to be up late is to be up late.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: A false conclusion. I hate it as an unfilled can. To be up after midnight, and to go to bed then, is early; so that to go to bed after midnight, is to go to bed betimes. Does not our life consist of the four elements?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Faith, so they say, but I think it rather consists of eating and drinking.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Th'art a scholar; let us therefore eat and drink. [Calling] Marian, I say, a stoup of wine!

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Here comes the fool, i'faith.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: How now, my hearts! Did you never see the picture of "We Three"?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Welcome, ass. Now let's have a catch.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: By my troth, the fool has an excellent breast. I had rather than forty shillings I had such a leg, and so sweet a breath to sing, as the fool has. In sooth, thou wast in very gracious fooling last night, when thou spok'st of Pigrogromitus, of the Vapians passing the equinoctial of Queubus. 'Twas very good, i'faith. I sent thee sixpence for thy leman—hadst it?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: I did impeticos thy gratillity: for Malvolio's nose is no whipstock, my lady has a white hand, and the Myrmidons are no bottle-ale houses.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Excellent! Why, this is the best fooling, when all is done. Now a song!

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [To Clown, giving money] Come on, there is sixpence for you. Let's have a song.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: [Giving sixpence] There's a testril of me too. If one knight give a—

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Would you have a love song, or a song of good life?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: A love song, a love song.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Ay, ay. I care not for good life.

lg.l: O mistress mine, where are you roaming?
O stay and hear, your true love's coming,
That can sing both high and low.
Trip no further, pretty sweeting,
Journeys end in lovers meeting,
Every wise man's son doth know.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Excellent good, i'faith.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Good, good.

lg.l: What is love? 'Tis not hereafter,
Present mirth hath present laughter;
What's to come is still unsure.
In delay there lies no plenty,
Then come kiss me, sweet and twenty;
Youth's a stuff will not endure.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: A mellifluous voice, as I am true knight.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: A contagious breath.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Very sweet and contagious, i'faith.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: To hear by the nose, it is dulcet in contagion. But shall we make the welkin dance indeed? Shall we rouse the night-owl in a catch that will draw three souls out of one weaver? Shall we do that?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: An you love me, let's do't! I am dog at a catch.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: By'r lady, sir, and some dogs will catch well.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Most certain. Let our catch be "Thou Knave."

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: "Hold thy peace, thou knave," knight? I shall be constrained in't to call thee knave, knight.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: 'Tis not the first time I have constrained one to call me knave. Begin, fool. It begins, [Singing] "Hold thy peace."

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: I shall never begin if I hold my peace.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Good, i'faith! Come, begin.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: What a caterwauling do you keep here! If my lady have not called up her steward Malvolio, and bid him turn you out of doors, never trust me.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: My lady's a Cathayan, we are politicians, Malvolio's a Peg-a-Ramsay, and [Singing] "Three merry men be we"! Am not I consanguineous? Am I not of her blood? Tilly-vally, lady! [Singing] "There dwelt a man in Babylon, lady, lady"!

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Beshrew me, the knight's in admirable fooling.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Ay, he does well enough if he be disposed, and so do I too. He does it with a better grace, but I do it more natural.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [Singing] "O'the twelfth day of December—"

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: For the love o'god, peace!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: My masters, are you mad! Or what are you? Have you no wit, manners, nor honesty, but to gabble like tinkers at this time of night? Do ye make an alehouse of my lady's house, that ye squeak out your coziers' catches without any mitigation or remorse of voice? Is there no respect of place, persons, nor time in you?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: We did keep time, sir, in our catches. Sneck up!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Sir Toby, I must be round with you. My lady bade me tell you that, though she harbors you as her kinsman, she's nothing allied to your disorders. If you can separate yourself and your misdemeanors, you are welcome to the house. If not, an it would please you to take leave of her, she is very willing to bid you farewell.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [Singing] [To Maria] "Farewell, dear heart, since I must needs be gone."

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Nay, good Sir Toby.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: [Singing] [Indicating Sir Toby] "His eyes do show his days are almost done."

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Is't even so?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [Singing] "But I will never die."

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: [Singing] Sir Toby, there you lie.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: This is much credit to you.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [Singing] [Indicating Malvolio] "Shall I bid him go?"

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: [Singing] "What an if you do?"

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [Singing] "Shall I bid him go, and spare not?"

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: [Singing] "O no, no, no, no, you dare not!"

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [To Malvolio] Out o'tune, sir? Ye lie! Art any more than a steward? Dost thou think because thou art virtuous there shall be no more cakes and ale?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Yes, by Saint Anne, and ginger shall be hot i'th'mouth too.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Th'art i'th'right. [To Malvolio] Go, sir, rub your chain with crumbs. A stoup of wine, Maria!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Mistress Mary, if you prized my lady's favor at anything more than contempt, you would not give means for this uncivil rule. She shall know of it, by this hand.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Go shake your ears!

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: 'Twere as good a deed as to drink when a man's a-hungry, to challenge him the field, and then to break promise with him, and make a fool of him.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Do't, knight. I'll write thee a challenge; or I'll deliver thy indignation to him by word of mouth.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Sweet Sir Toby, be patient for tonight. Since the youth of the count's was today with my lady, she is much out of quiet. For Monsieur Malvolio, let me alone with him. If I do not gull him into a nayword, and make him a common recreation, do not think I have wit enough to lie straight in my bed. I know I can do it.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Possess us, possess us, tell us something of him.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Marry, sir, sometimes he is a kind of puritan.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Oh, if I thought that, I'd beat him like a dog!

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: What, for being a puritan? Thy exquisite reason, dear knight?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: I have no exquisite reason for't, but I have reason good enough.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: The devil a puritan that he is, or anything constantly but a time-pleaser, an affectioned ass, that cons state without book, and utters it by great swaths. The best persuaded of himself, so crammed, as he thinks, with excellencies, that it is his grounds of faith that all that look on him love him; and on that vice in him will my revenge find notable cause to work.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: What wilt thou do?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: I will drop in his way some obscure epistles of love, wherein by the color of his beard, the shape of his leg, the manner of his gait, the expressure of his eye, forehead, and complexion, he shall find himself most feelingly personated. I can write very like my lady your niece; on a forgotten matter we can hardly make distinction of our hands.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Excellent, I smell a device.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: I have't in my nose too.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: He shall think by the letters that thou wilt drop that they come from my niece, and that she's in love with him.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: My purpose is indeed a horse of that color.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: And your horse now would make him an ass.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Ass, I doubt not.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Oh, 'twill be admirable!

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Sport royal, I warrant you. I know my physic will work with him. I will plant you two, and let the fool make a third, where he shall find the letter. Observe his construction of it. For this night, to bed, and dream on the event. Farewell.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Good night, Penthesilea!

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Before me, she's a good wench.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: She's a beagle true bred, and one that adores me. What o'that?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: I was adored once, too.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Let's to bed, knight. Thou hadst need send for more money.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: If I cannot recover your niece, I am a foul way out.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Send for money, knight. If thou hast her not i'th'end, call me cut.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: If I do not, never trust me, take it how you will.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Come, come, I'll go burn some sack; 'tis too late to go to bed now. Come, knight, come, knight.

div2.stage: Enter Orsino, Viola [as Cesario], Curio, and others.

lg.l: [To the Musicians] Give me some music. [To the Courtiers] Now good morrow, friends;
Now, good Cesario—but that piece of song,
That old and antique song we heard last night;
Methought it did relieve my passion much,
More than light airs and recollected terms
Of these most brisk and giddy-pacèd times.
Come, but one verse.

sp.speaker: CURIO
sp.p: He is not here, so please your lordship, that should sing it.

sp.speaker: ORSINO
sp.p: Who was it?

sp.speaker: CURIO
sp.p: Feste the jester, my lord, a fool that the Lady Olivia's father took much delight in. He is about the house.

sp.speaker: ORSINO
sp.p: Seek him out, [To the Musicians] and play the tune the while.

lg.l: Come hither, boy. If ever thou shalt love,
In the sweet pangs of it, remember me.
For such as I am, all true lovers are:
Unstaid and skittish in all motions else,
Save in the constant image of the creature
That is beloved. How dost thou like this tune?
It gives a very echo to the seat
Where love is throned.
Thou dost speak masterly;
My life upon't, young though thou art, thine eye
Hath stayed upon some favor that it loves.
Hath it not, boy?
A little, by your favor.
What kind of woman is't?
Of your complexion.
She is not worth thee then. What years, i'faith?
About your years, my lord.
Too old, by heaven! Let still the woman take
An elder than her self; so wears she to him,
So sways she level in her husband's heart.
For, boy, however we do praise ourselves,
Our fancies are more giddy and unfirm,
More longing, wavering, sooner lost and worn,
Than women's are.
I think it well, my lord.
Then let thy love be younger than thyself,
Or thy affection cannot hold the bent;
For women are as roses, whose fair flower
Being once displayed, doth fall that very hour.
And so they are. Alas, that they are so:
To die, even when they to perfection grow.
Oh, fellow, come, the song we had last night.
Mark it, Cesario, it is old and plain;
The spinsters and the knitters in the sun,
And the free maids that weave their thread with bones,
Do use to chant it. It is silly sooth,
And dallies with the innocence of love,
Like the old age.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Are you ready, sir?

lg.l: Ay, prithee sing.
[Singing] Come away, come away, death,
And in sad cypress let me be laid.
Fie away, fie away, breath,
I am slain by a fair cruel maid.
My shroud of white, stuck all with yew,
O prepare it.
My part of death no one so true
Did share it.
Not a flower, not a flower sweet,
On my Black Coffin let there be strewn.
Not a friendo, not a friendo greet
My poor corpse, where my bones shall be thrown.
A thousand, thousand sights to save,
Lay me O where
Sad true lover never find my grave,
To weep there.
[Giving money] There's for thy pains.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: No pains, sir; I take pleasure in singing, sir.

lg.l: I'll pay thy pleasure then.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Truly, sir, and pleasure will be paid, one time or another.

lg.l: Give me now leave to leave thee.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Now the melancholy god protect thee, and the tailor make thy doublet of changeable taffeta, for thy mind is a very opal. I would have men of such constancy put to sea, that their business might be everything, and their intent everywhere; for that's it that always makes a good voyage of nothing. Farewell.

lg.l: Let all the rest give place.
lg.stage: [All the Courtiers except Viola stand apart.]
lg.l: Once more, Cesario,
Get thee to yond same sovereign cruelty.
Tell her my love, more noble than the world,
Prizes not quantity of dirty lands;
The parts that Fortune hath bestowed upon her,
Tell her I hold as giddily as Fortune;
But 'tis that miracle and queen of gems
That Nature pranks her in, attracts my soul.
But if she cannot love you, sir?
I cannot be so answered.
Sooth, but you must.
Say that some lady, as perhaps there is,
Hath for your love as great a pang of heart
As you have for Olivia. You cannot love her.
You tell her so. Must she not then be answered?
There is no woman's sides
Can bide the beating of so strong a passion
As love doth give my heart; no woman's heart
So big, to hold so much. They lack retention.
Alas, their love may be called appetite,
No motion of the liver, but the palate,
That suffers surfeit, cloyment, and revolt;
But mine is all as hungry as the sea,
And can digest as much. Make no compare
Between that love a woman can bear me,
And that I owe Olivia.
Ay, but I know—
What dost thou know?
Too well what love women to men may owe.
In faith, they are as true of heart as we.
My father had a daughter loved a man
As it might be perhaps, were I a woman,
I should your lordship.
And what's her history?
A blank, my lord. She never told her love,
But let concealment like a worm i'th'bud
Feed on her damask cheek. She pined in thought,
And with a green and yellow melancholy
She sat like Patience on a monument,
Smiling at grief. Was not this love indeed?
We men may say more, swear more, but indeed
Our shows are more than will: for still we prove
Much in our vows, but little in our love.
But died thy sister of her love, my boy?
I am all the daughters of my father's house,
And all the brothers too; and yet I know not—
Sir, shall I to this lady?
Ay, that's the theme.
To her in haste; [Giving a jewel] give her this jewel; say
My love can give no place, bide no denay.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Toby, Sir Andrew, and Fabian.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Come thy ways, Signor Fabian.

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: Nay, I'll come! If I lose a scruple of this sport, let me be boiled to death with melancholy.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Wouldst thou not be glad to have the niggardly rascally sheep-biter come by some notable shame?

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: I would exult, man! You know he brought me out o'favor with my lady, about a bear-baiting here.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: To anger him we'll have the bear again, and we will fool him black and blue—shall we not, Sir Andrew?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: An we do not, it is pity of our lives.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Here comes the little villain! How now, my metal of India?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Get ye all three into the box-tree. Malvolio's coming down this walk; he has been yonder i'the sun practicing behavior to his own shadow this half hour. Observe him, for the love of mockery, for I know this letter will make a contemplative idiot of him. Close, in the name of jesting! [The men hide.] Lie thou there; [Placing the letter on the stage] for here comes the trout that must be caught with tickling.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: [To the audience] 'Tis but fortune, all is fortune. Maria once told me she did affect me, and I have heard herself come thus near, that should she fancy, it should be one of my complexion. Besides, she uses me with a more exalted respect than anyone else that follows her. What should I think on't?

p.seg: Here's an overweening rogue!
Oh, peace! Contemplation makes a rare turkey-cock of him; how he jets under his advanced plumes!
'Slight, I could so beat the rogue!
Peace, I say!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: To be Count Malvolio!

p.seg: Ah, rogue!
Pistol him, pistol him!
Peace, peace!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: There is example for't: the Lady of the Strachy married the yeoman of the wardrobe.

p.seg: Fie on him, Jezebel!
Oh, peace, now he's deeply in. Look how imagination blows him.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Having been three months married to her, sitting in my state—

p.seg: Oh, for a stone-bow to hit him in the eye!
—calling my officers about me, in my branched velvet gown, having come from a day-bed, where I have left Olivia sleeping—
Fire and brimstone!
Oh, peace, peace!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: —and then to have the humor of state, and after a demure travel of regard—telling them I know my place, as I would they should do theirs—to ask for my kinsman Toby.

p.seg: Bolts and shackles!
Oh, peace, peace, peace! Now, now!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Seven of my people, with an obedient start, make out for him. I frown the while, and perchance wind up my watch, or play with my— [Realizing he is playing with his steward's chain] some rich jewel. Toby approaches; curtsies there to me—

p.seg: Shall this fellow live!
Though our silence be drawn from us with cars, yet peace!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: —I extend my hand to him, thus; quenching my familiar smile with an austere regard of control—

p.seg: And does not Toby take you a blow o'the lips then?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: —saying, "Cousin Toby, my fortunes having cast me on your niece give me this prerogative of speech—"

p.seg: What, what!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "—you must amend your drunkenness."

p.seg: Out, scab!
Nay, patience, or we break the sinews of our plot!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "Besides, you waste the treasure of your time with a foolish knight—"

p.seg: That's me, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "—one Sir Andrew."

p.seg: I knew 'twas I, for many do call me fool.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: [Seeing and then taking up the letter] What employment have we here?

p.seg: Now is the woodcock near the gin.
Oh, peace, and the spirit of humors intimate reading aloud to him.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: [To the audience, as he examines the outside of the letter] By my life, this is my lady's hand: these be her very C's, her U's, and her T's, and thus makes she her great P's. It is, in contempt of question, her hand.

p.seg: Her C's, her U's, and her T's

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: [Reading] "To the unknown belovèd, this, and my good wishes." Her very phrases! [Starting to break the seal] By your leave, wax. [Pausing] Soft! And the impressure her Lucrece, with which she uses to seal. 'Tis my lady! To whom should this be?

div2.stage: [He breaks the seal and opens the letter.]

p.seg: This wins him, liver and all.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO

lg.l: "Jove knows I love,

sp.p: But who? Lips, do not move, No man must know." "No man must know." What follows? The numbers altered. "No man must know." If this should be thee, Malvolio!

p.seg: Marry, hang thee, brock!

lg.l: [Reading] "I may command, where I adore,
But silence, like a Lucrece knife,
With bloodless stroke my heart doth gore;
M.O.A.I. doth sway my life."

p.seg: A fustian riddle.
Excellent wench, say I.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "M.O.A.I. doth sway my life." Nay, but first let me see, let me see, let me see.

p.seg: What dish o'poison has she dressed him!
And with what wing the staniel checks at it!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "I may command, where I adore." Why, she may command me: I serve her, she is my lady. Why, this is evident to any formal capacity. There is no obstruction in this. And the end—what should that alphabetical position portend? If I could make that resemble something in me! Softly. "M.O.A.I."

p.seg: Oh, ay, make up that! He is now at a cold scent.
Sowter will cry upon't for all this, though it be as rank as a fox.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "M." Malvolio! "M," why that begins my name!

p.seg: Did not I say he would work it out? The cur is excellent at faults.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "M." But then there is no consonancy in the sequel. That suffers under probation: "A" should follow, but "O" does.

p.seg: And "O" shall end, I hope.
Ay, or I'll cudgel him, and make him cry "O"!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: And then "I" comes behind.

p.seg: Ay, an you had any eye behind you, you might see more detraction at your heels than fortunes before you.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "M.O.A.I." This simulation is not as the former; and yet to crush this a little, it would bow to me, for every one of these letters are in my name. Soft, here follows prose.

lg.l: "If this fall into thy hand, revolve. In my stars I am above thee, but be not afraid of greatness. Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em. Thy fates open their hands, let thy blood and spirit embrace them; and to inure thyself to what thou art like to be, cast thy humble slough, and appear fresh. Be opposite with a kinsman, surly with servants; let thy tongue tang arguments of state; put thyself into the trick of singularity. She thus advises thee, that sighs for thee. Remember who commended thy yellow stockings, and wished to see thee ever cross-gartered. I say remember. Go to, thou art made if thou desir'st to be so. If not, let me see thee a steward still, the fellow of servants, and not worthy to touch Fortune's fingers. Farewell.
She that would alter services with thee,
The Fortunate-Unhappy."

Daylight and champaign discovers not more! This is open. I will be proud, I will read politic authors, I will baffle Sir Toby, I will wash off gross acquaintance, I will be point-device the very man. I do not now fool myself, to let imagination jade me; for every reason excites to this, that my lady loves me. She did commend my yellow stockings of late, she did praise my leg being cross-gartered, and in this she manifests herself to my love, and with a kind of injunction drives me to these habits of her liking. I thank my stars, I am happy. I will be strange, stout, in yellow stockings, and cross-gartered, even with the swiftness of putting on. Jove and my stars be praised! Here is yet a postscript.
"Thou canst not choose but know who I am. If thou entertain'st my love, let it appear in thy smiling; thy smiles become thee well. Therefore in my presence still smile, dear my sweet, I prithee."

sp.p: Jove, I thank thee. I will smile, I will do everything that thou wilt have me.

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: I will not give my part of this sport for a pension of thousands to be paid from the Sophy.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: I could marry this wench for this device—

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: So could I too.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: —and ask no other dowry with her, but such another jest.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Nor I neither.

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: Here comes my noble gull-catcher.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [Abasing himself on the stage] Wilt thou set thy foot o'my neck?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: [Following suit as Sir Toby rises] Or o'mine either?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Shall I play my freedom at tray-trip, and become thy bondslave?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: I'faith, or I either?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Why, thou hast put him in such a dream that when the image of it leaves him he must run mad.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Nay, but say true, does it work upon him?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Like aqua-vitae with a midwife.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: If you will then see the fruits of the sport, mark his first approach before my lady. He will come to her in yellow stockings, and 'tis a color she abhors, and cross-gartered, a fashion she detests; and he will smile upon her, which will now be so unsuitable to her disposition, being addicted to a melancholy as she is, that it cannot but turn him into a notable contempt. If you will see it, follow me.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: To the gates of Tartarus, thou most excellent devil of wit!

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: I'll make one too.

div2.stage: Enter [from different ways] Viola [as Cesario] and Clown [playing on tabor and pipe].

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Save thee, friend, and thy music. Dost thou live by thy tabor?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: No, sir, I live by the church.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Art thou a churchman?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: No such matter, sir. I do live by the church, for I do live at my house, and my house doth stand by the church.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: So thou mayst say the king lies by a beggar, if a beggar dwell near him; or the church stands by thy tabor, if thy tabor stand by the church.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: You have said, sir. [To the audience as well as Viola] To see this age! A sentence is but a cheverel glove to a good wit: how quickly the wrong side may be turned outward!

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Nay, that's certain: they that dally nicely with words may quickly make them wanton.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: I would therefore my sister had had no name, sir.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Why, man?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Why, sir, her name's a word, and to dally with that word might make my sister wanton. But indeed, words are very rascals since bonds disgraced them.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Thy reason, man?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Troth, sir, I can yield you none without words, and words are grown so false I am loath to prove reason with them.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: I warrant thou art a merry fellow and car'st for nothing.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Not so, sir, I do care for something; but in my conscience, sir, I do not care for you: if that be to care for nothing, sir, I would it would make you invisible.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Art not thou the Lady Olivia's fool?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: No indeed, sir! The Lady Olivia has no folly. She will keep no fool, sir, till she be married; and fools are as like husbands as pilchards are to herrings: the husband's the bigger. I am indeed not her fool, but her corrupter of words.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: I saw thee late at the Count Orsino's.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Foolery, sir, does walk about the orb like the sun, it shines everywhere. I would be sorry, sir, but the fool should be as oft with your master as with my mistress: I think I saw your wisdom there.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Nay, an thou pass upon me, I'll no more with thee. Hold, [Giving him a coin] there's expenses for thee.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: Now Jove, in his next commodity of hair, send thee a beard.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: By my troth, I'll tell thee, I am almost sick for one, [To the audience] though I would not have it grow on my chin. [To the Clown.] Is thy lady within?

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: [Indicating the coin] Would not a pair of these have bred, sir?

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: Yes, being kept together, and put to use.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: I would play Lord Pandarus of Phrygia, sir, to bring a Cressida to [Displaying the coin] this Troilus.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: [Gives another coin.] I understand you, sir, 'tis well begged.

sp.speaker: CLOWN
sp.p: The matter, I hope, is not great, sir, begging but a beggar: Cressida was a beggar. My lady is within, sir. I will conster to them whence you come; who you are, and what you would, are out of my welkin—I might say element, but the word is overworn.

lg.l: [To the audience] This fellow is wise enough to play the fool,
And to do that well craves a kind of wit.
He must observe their mood on whom he jests,
The quality of persons, and the time;
And like the haggard, check at every feather
That comes before his eye. This is a practice
As full of labor as a wise man's art:
For folly that he wisely shows, is fit;
But wise men, folly-fall'n, quite taint their wit.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Toby and Sir Andrew.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Save you, gentleman.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: And you, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: I hope, sir, you are, and I am yours.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Will you encounter the house? My niece is desirous you should enter, if your trade be to her.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: I am bound to your niece, sir; I mean, she is the list of my voyage.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Taste your legs, sir, put them to motion.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: My legs do better understand me, sir, than I understand what you mean by bidding me taste my legs.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: I mean to go, sir, to enter.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: I will answer you with gait and entrance— Enter Olivia and [Maria]. But we are prevented. [To Olivia] Most excellent accomplished lady, the heavens rain odors on you.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: [To the audience] That youth's a rare courtier: "rain odors"—well.

sp.speaker: VIOLA
sp.p: My matter hath no voice, lady, but to your own most pregnant and vouchsafed ear.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: [Writing] "Odors," "pregnant," and "vouchsafed": I'll get 'em all three all ready.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Let the garden door be shut, and leave me to my hearing.
sp.stage: [Exeunt Maria and Sir Toby, followed by Sir Andrew] [observing Olivia.]

lg.l: Give me your hand, sir.

div2.stage: [Viola kneels instead to kiss Olivia's hand.]

lg.l: My duty, madam, and most humble service.
What is your name?
Cesario is your servant's name, fair princess.
My servant, sir? 'Twas never merry world
Since lowly feigning was called compliment.
Y'are servant to the Count Orsino, youth.
And he is yours, and his must needs be yours:
Your servant's servant is your servant, madam.
For him, I think not on him; for his thoughts,
Would they were blanks, rather than filled with me.
Madam, I come to whet your gentle thoughts
On his behalf.
Oh, by your leave, I pray you!
I bade you never speak again of him;
But would you undertake another suit,
I had rather hear you to solicit that
Than music from the spheres.
Dear lady—
Give me leave, beseech you. I did send,
After the last enchantment you did here,
A ring in chase of you. So did I abuse
Myself, my servant, and I fear me, you.
Under your hard construction must I sit,
To force that on you in a shameful cunning
Which you knew none of yours. What might you think?
Have you not set mine honor at the stake,
And baited it with all th'unmuzzled thoughts
That tyrannous heart can think? To one of your receiving
Enough is shown; a cypress, not a bosom,
Hides my heart. So, let me hear you speak.
I pity you.
That's a degree to love.
No, not a grece: for 'tis a vulgar proof
That very oft we pity enemies.
Why then, methinks 'tis time to smile again.
O world, how apt the poor are to be proud!
If one should be a prey, how much the better
To fall before the lion than the wolf!
The clock upbraids me with the waste of time.
Be not afraid, good youth, I will not have you;
And yet when wit and youth is come to harvest,
Your wife is like to reap a proper man.
There lies your way, due west.
Then westward ho!
Grace and good disposition attend your ladyship.
You'll nothing, madam, to my lord by me?
Stay!
I prithee tell me what thou think'st of me?
That you do think you are not what you are.
If I think so, I think the same of you.
Then think you right: [Including the audience] I am not what I am.
I would you were as I would have you be.
Would it be better, madam, than I am?
I wish it might, for now I am your fool!
[To the audience] Oh, what a deal of scorn looks beautiful
In the contempt and anger of his lip!
A murd'rous guilt shows not itself more soon,
Than love that would seem hid. Love's night is noon.
[To Viola] Cesario, by the roses of the spring,
By maidhood, honor, truth, and everything,
I love thee so, that maugre all thy pride,
Nor wit nor reason can my passion hide.
Do not extort thy reasons from this clause,
For that I woo, thou therefore hast no cause;
But rather reason thus with reason fetter:
Love sought is good, but giv'n unsought is better.
By innocence I swear, and by my youth,
I have one heart, one bosom, and one truth,
And that no woman has; nor never none
Shall mistress be of it, save I alone.
And so adieu, good madam; never more
Will I my master's tears to you deplore.
Yet come again—for thou perhaps mayst move
That heart, which now abhors, to like his love.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Andrew, [followed by] Sir Toby and Fabian.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: No, faith, I'll not stay a jot longer!

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Thy reason, dear venom, give thy reason.

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: You must needs yield your reason, Sir Andrew!

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Marry, I saw your niece do more favors to the count's serving-man than ever she bestowed upon me. I saw't i'th'orchard.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Did she see thee the while, old boy, tell me that?

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: As plain as I see you now.

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: This was a great argument of love in her toward you.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: 'Slight, will you make an ass o'me?

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: I will prove it legitimate, sir, upon the oaths of judgment and reason.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: And they have been grand-jurymen since before Noah was a sailor.

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: She did show favor to the youth in your sight only to exasperate you, to awake your dormouse valor, to put fire in your heart, and brimstone in your liver. You should then have accosted her, and with some excellent jests, fire-new from the mint, you should have banged the youth into dumbness. This was looked for at your hand, and this was balked. The double gilt of this opportunity you let time wash off, and you are now sailed into the north of my lady's opinion, where you will hang like an icicle on a Dutchman's beard, unless you do redeem it by some laudable attempt, either of valor or policy.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: An't be any way, it must be with valor, for policy I hate. [To the audience] I had as lief be a Brownist, as a politician.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Why then, build me thy fortunes upon the basis of valor. Challenge me the count's youth to fight with him, hurt him in eleven places. My niece shall take note of it; and assure thyself, there is no love-broker in the world can more prevail in man's commendation with women than report of valor.

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: There is no way but this, Sir Andrew.

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Will either of you bear me a challenge to him?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Go, write it in a martial hand. Be cursed and brief. It is no matter how witty, so it be eloquent, and full of invention. Taunt him with the license of ink. If thou "thou'st" him some thrice, it shall not be amiss; and as many lies as will lie in thy sheet of paper, although the sheet were big enough for the bed of Ware in England, set 'em down. Go, about it! Let there be gall enough in thy ink; though thou write with a goose-pen, no matter. About it!

sp.speaker: SIR ANDREW
sp.p: Where shall I find you?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: We'll call thee at thy cubiculo . Go!

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: This is a dear manikin to you, Sir Toby.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: I have been dear to him, lad, some two thousand strong, or so.

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: We shall have a rare letter from him—but you'll not deliver't?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Never trust me then; and by all means stir on the youth to an answer. I think oxen and wainropes cannot hale them together. For Andrew, if he were opened and you find so much blood in his liver as will clog the foot of a flea, I'll eat the rest of th'anatomy.

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: And his opposite, the youth, bears in his visage no great presage of cruelty.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Look where the youngest wren of nine comes.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: If you desire the spleen, and will laugh your selves into stitches, follow me. Yond gull Malvolio is turned heathen, a very renegado; for there is no Christian that means to be saved by believing rightly can ever believe such impossible passages of grossness. He's in yellow stockings!

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: And cross-gartered?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Most villainously, like a pedant that keeps a school i'th'church. I have dogged him like his murderer. He does obey every point of the letter that I dropped to betray him. He does smile his face into more lines than is in the new map with the augmentation of the Indies; you have not seen such a thing as 'tis. I can hardly forbear hurling things at him; I know my lady will strike him. If she do, he'll smile, and take't for a great favor.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Come, bring us, bring us where he is!

lg.l: I would not by my will have troubled you,
But since you make your pleasure of your pains,
I will no further chide you.
I could not stay behind you. My desire,
More sharp than filèd steel, did spur me forth;
And not all love to see you—though so much
As might have drawn one to a longer voyage—
But jealousy what might befall your travel,
Being skilless in these parts, which to a stranger,
Unguided and unfriended, often prove
Rough and unhospitable. My willing love,
The rather by these arguments of fear,
Set forth in your pursuit.
My kind Antonio,
I can no other answer make but thanks,
And thanks, and ever thanks; and oft good turns
Are shuffled off with such uncurrent pay.
But were my worth, as is my conscience, firm,
You should find better dealing. What's to do?
Shall we go see the relics of this town?
Tomorrow, sir; best first go see your lodging.
I am not weary, and 'tis long to night.
I pray you, let us satisfy our eyes
With the memorials and the things of fame
That do renown this city.
Would you'd pardon me.
I do not without danger walk these streets.
Once in a sea-fight 'gainst the count his galleys
I did some service, of such note indeed
That were I ta'en here it would scarce be answered.
Belike you slew great number of his people.
Th'offence is not of such a bloody nature,
Albeit the quality of the time and quarrel
Might well have given us bloody argument.
It might have since been answered in repaying
What we took from them, which for traffic's sake
Most of our city did. Only myself stood out,
For which, if I be lapsèd in this place,
I shall pay dear.
Do not then walk too open.
It doth not fit me. Hold, sir, here's my purse.
In the south suburbs at the Elephant
Is best to lodge; I will bespeak our diet,
Whiles you beguile the time, and feed your knowledge
With viewing of the town. There shall you have me.
Why I your purse?
Haply your eye shall light upon some toy
You have desire to purchase; and your store,
I think, is not for idle markets, sir.
I'll be your purse-bearer, and leave you for
An hour.
To th'Elephant.
I do remember.
[To the audience] I have sent after him; he says he'll come.
How shall I feast him? What bestow of him?
For youth is bought more oft than begged or borrowed.
I speak too loud—
[To Maria] Where's Malvolio? He is sad and civil,
And suits well for a servant with my fortunes.
Where is Malvolio?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: He's coming, madam, but in very strange manner. He is sure possessed, madam.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Why, what's the matter? Does he rave?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: No, madam, he does nothing but smile. Your ladyship were best to have some guard about you if he come, for sure the man is tainted in's wits.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA

lg.l: Go call him hither. [Maria starts to exit.] I am as mad as he,
If sad and merry madness equal be.

sp.p: How now, Malvolio!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Sweet lady, ho, ho!

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Smil'st thou? I sent for thee upon a sad occasion.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Sad, lady? I could be sad. This does make some obstruction in the blood, this cross-gartering; but what of that? If it please the eye of one, it is with me as the very true sonnet is, [Singing] "Please one, and please all."

div2.stage: [He kisses his hand to her repeatedly.]

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Why, how dost thou, man? What is the matter with thee?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Not black in my mind, though yellow in my legs. [Holding up letter] It did come to his hands, and commands shall be executed. I think we do know the sweet roman hand.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Wilt thou go to bed, Malvolio?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: To bed! [Singing] "Ay, sweetheart, and I'll come to thee."

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: God comfort thee! Why dost thou smile so, and kiss thy hand so oft?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: How do you, Malvolio?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: [To Maria, scornfully] At your request? Yes, nightingales answer daws!

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: Why appear you with this ridiculous boldness before my lady?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: [To Olivia] "Be not afraid of greatness": 'twas well writ.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: What mean'st thou by that, Malvolio?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "Some are born great—"

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Ha?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "—some achieve greatness—"

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: What say'st thou?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "—and some have greatness thrust upon them."

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Heaven restore thee!

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "Remember who commended thy yellow stockings—"

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Thy yellow stockings?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "—and wished to see thee cross-gartered."

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Cross-gartered?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "Go to, thou art made, if thou desir'st to be so—"

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: Am I made?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: "—if not, let me see thee a servant still."

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: [To the audience] Why, this is very midsummer madness.

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: Madam, the young gentleman of the Count Orsino's is returned; I could hardly entreat him back. He attends your ladyship's pleasure.

sp.speaker: OLIVIA
sp.p: I'll come to him. [Exit Servant.] Good Maria, let this fellow be looked to. Where's my cousin Toby? Let some of my people have a special care of him; I would not have him miscarry for the half of my dowry.

div2.stage: Exit [following Servant, Maria a different way].

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Oh ho, do you come near me now? [To the audience] No worse man than Sir Toby to look to me! This concurs directly with the letter. She sends him on purpose, that I may appear stubborn to him; for she incites me to that in the letter. "Cast thy humble slough," says she, "be opposite with a kinsman, surly with servants, let thy tongue tang with arguments of state, put thyself into the trick of singularity"; and consequently sets down the manner how: as, a sad face, a reverend carriage, a slow tongue, in the habit of some sir of note, and so forth. I have limed her, but it is Jove's doing, and Jove make me thankful. And when she went away now, "Let this fellow be looked to." "Fellow!" Not Malvolio, nor after my degree, but "fellow." Why, everything adheres together, that no dram of a scruple, no scruple of a scruple, no obstacle, no incredulous or unsafe circumstance—what can be said? Nothing that can be can come between me and the full prospect of my hopes. Well Jove, not I, is the doer of this, and he is to be thanked.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Toby, Fabian, and Maria.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [Pretending not to see Malvolio] Which way is he, in the name of sanctity? If all the devils of hell be drawn in little, and Legion himself possessed him, yet I'll speak to him.

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: Here he is, here he is. [To Malvolio] How is't with you, sir? How is't with you, man?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Go off, I discard you. Let me enjoy my private. Go off!

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: [To Sir Toby and Fabian, aloud, to be overheard] Lo, how hollow the fiend speaks within him! Did not I tell you? Sir Toby, my lady prays you to have a care of him.

p.seg: Ah ha! Does she so?

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [To them, aloud] Go to, go to. Peace, peace, we must deal gently with him. Let me alone. [Approaching Malvolio] How do you, Malvolio? How is't with you? What, man, defy the devil; consider, he's an enemy to mankind.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Do you know what you say?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: [To them, aloud] La you, an you speak ill of the devil, how he takes it at heart! Pray God he be not bewitched!

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: [To them, aloud] Carry his water to th'wise woman.

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: [To them, aloud] Marry, and it shall be done tomorrow morning if I live. My lady would not lose him for more than I'll say.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: How now, mistress?

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: [To them, aloud] Oh Lord!

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [To them, aloud] Prithee hold thy peace, this is not the way. Do you not see you move him? Let me alone with him.

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: [To them, aloud] No way but gentleness; gently, gently. The fiend is rough, and will not be roughly used.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [Approaching Malvolio] Why, how now, my bawcock? How dost thou, chuck?

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Sir!

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: Ay, biddy, come with me. What, man, 'tis not for gravity to play at cherry-pit with Satan. Hang him, foul collier!

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: [To them, aloud] Get him to say his prayers, good Sir Toby, get him to pray.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: My prayers, minx!

sp.speaker: MARIA
sp.p: [To them, aloud] No, I warrant you, he will not hear of godliness.

sp.speaker: MALVOLIO
sp.p: Go hang yourselves all! You are idle, shallow things; I am not of your element. You shall know more hereafter.

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
sp.p: [Laughing] Is't possible?

sp.speaker: FABIAN
sp.p: [Including the audience] If this were played upon a stage now, I could condemn it as an improbable fiction!

sp.speaker: SIR TOBY
